claim: Sparse, sequential patterns of neural activity have been observed in cortex during timekeeping and motor sequence tasks.
source: Sparse, sequential patterns of neural activity have been observed in numerous brain areas during timekeeping and motor sequence tasks. Inspired by such observations, we construct a model of the striatum, an all-inhibitory circuit where sequential activity patterns are prominent, addressing the following key challenges: (i) obtaining control over temporal rescaling of the sequence speed, with the ability to generalize to new speeds; (ii) facilitating flexible expression of distinct sequences via selective activation, concatenation, and recycling of specific subsequences; and (iii) enabling the biologically plausible learning of sequences, consistent with the decoupling of learning and execution suggested by lesion studies showing that cortical circuits are necessary for learning, but that subcortical circuits are sufficient to drive learned behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Luczak et al., 2007; Jin et al., 2009; Harvey et al., 2012) that observed these patterns.

claim: Neural activity sequences have been shown to temporally rescale as behavior speeds up and slows down.
source: First, these sequences have been shown to temporally rescale (i.e., contract and dilate) as behavior speeds up and slows down (Mello et al., 2015; Gouvêa et al., 2015), while human psychophysics experiments have shown that after learning a behavior (e.g., an arm reach trajectory) at one speed of execution, it can be reliably expressed at other speeds without additional learning (Goodbody and Wolpert, 1998; Joiner et al., 2011; Shmuelof et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Mello et al., 2015; Gouvêa et al., 2015) that demonstrated temporal rescaling.

claim: Sparse activity sequences have been observed in recurrently connected populations of inhibitory medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in rodents during locomotion.
source: Although the basic mechanisms that we propose may be realized in any brain area where sequences have been observed, for a specific example and to compare to experimental results, we focus on neural activity in striatum, where sparse activity sequences have been observed in recurrently connected populations of inhibitory medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in rodents during locomotion (Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015) and lever-press delay tasks (Mello et al., 2015; Dhawale et al., 2015; Gouvêa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an experimental study (Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015).

source: The striatum collects inputs from many areas of cortex and thalamus, plays an important part in controlling learned movements using its projections via the output structures of basal ganglia to motor thalamus and brainstem (Parent, 1990; Grillner and Robertson, 2015), and has a central role in reinforcement learning (Graybiel, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Parent, 1990; Grillner and Robertson, 2015).

claim: MSNs constitute over 90% of the neurons in striatum.
source: MSNs, which constitute over 90% of the neurons in striatum (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011), exhibit stereotyped sequential firing patterns during learned motor sequences and learned behaviors in which timing plays an important role, with sparse firing sequences providing a seemingly ideal representation for encoding time and providing a rich temporal basis that can be read out by downstream circuits to determine behavior (Jin et al., 2009; Mello et al., 2015; Rueda-Orozco and Robbe, 2015; Dhawale et al., 2015; Gouvêa et al., 2015; Bakhurin et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).

evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an experimental study (Gouvêa et al., 2015).

claim: Motor cortex is known to play a major role in both the learning and directing of motor behaviors such as limb movements in primates.
source: While motor cortex is also known to play a major role in both the learning and directing of motor behaviors such as limb movements in both primates (Fritsch and Hitzig, 1870; Georgopoulos et al., 1982, 1986; Moran and Schwartz, 1999; Kakei et al., 1999) and rodents (Wise and Donoghue, 1986; Kleim et al., 1998; Whishaw, 2000; Harrison et al., 2012), cortical lesion studies have long pointed to the ability of subcortical structures to direct a large repertoire of movements, particularly 'innate' movements and learned movements that don't require dexterous hand motion (Lawrence and Kuypers, 1968; Sorenson and Ellison, 1970; Bjursten et al., 1976; Passingham et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Fritsch and Hitzig, 1870; Georgopoulos et al., 1982, 1986; Moran and Schwartz, 1999; Kakei et al., 1999).

claim: Rats are unable to learn precisely timed lever-press sequences when motor cortex is lesioned.
source: Addressing the roles of cortical and striatal circuits in the learning and performance of motor skills, one set of recent studies has shown that rats are unable to learn precisely timed lever-press sequences when motor cortex is lesioned, but are able to successfully perform the sequence if the lesion occurs after the learning has already taken place (Kawai et al., 2015; Otchy et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Kawai et al., 2015; Otchy et al., 2015).

claim: Rats are able to successfully perform precisely timed lever-press sequences if the motor cortex lesion occurs after the learning has already taken place.

claim: Motor cortex may act as a 'tutor' to subcortical brain circuits during learning.
source: It was therefore suggested that motor cortex may act as a 'tutor' to subcortical brain circuits during learning, and that these lower brain circuits eventually internalize the activity pattern, allowing them to drive behavior without receiving further instruction from the tutor once the behavior has been learned (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a suggestion based on the cited experimental study (Kawai et al., 2015).

claim: Subcortical brain circuits eventually internalize the activity pattern, allowing them to drive behavior without receiving further instruction from the tutor once the behavior has been learned.
source: It was therefore suggested that motor cortex may act as a 'tutor' to subcortical brain circuits during learning, and that these lower brain circuits eventually internalize the activity pattern, allowing them to drive behavior without receiving further instruction from the tutor once the behavior has been learned (Kawai et al., 2015).

claim: Synaptic depression exists at the inhibitory synapses between MSNs.
source: A key element is the presence of synaptic depression at the inhibitory synapses between MSNs, which has been shown to exist experimentally (Tecuapetla et al., 2007) and which competes with the effect of feedforward excitatory input to determine the rate of switching of activity from one neuron cluster to the next.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an experimental study (Tecuapetla et al., 2007).

claim: Recurrent inhibition can lead to a winner-take-all steady state in which a single unit or group of units becomes active and inhibits the other units in the network from becoming active.
source: In order to achieve sparse activity, we make use of the well-known fact that recurrent inhibition can lead to a winner-take-all steady state in which a single unit or group of units (where a unit consists of a cluster of MSNs) becomes active and inhibits the other units in the network from becoming active.
evidence: The claim is described as a well-known fact, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Recurrent inhibition is a hallmark feature of MSNs in striatum.
source: Indeed, recurrent inhibition is a hallmark feature of MSNs in striatum, and such a picture has previously been suggested to apply to striatum (Wickens et al., 1991; Beiser and Houk, 1998; Fukai, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Wickens et al., 1991; Beiser and Houk, 1998; Fukai, 1999).

claim: Individual inhibitory synapses between MSNs are relatively sparse and weak on the scale of the currents needed to drive spiking in these neurons.
source: Although individual inhibitory synapses between MSNs are relatively sparse and weak on the scale of the currents needed to drive spiking in these neurons (Jaeger et al., 1994; Tepper et al., 2004), active populations of many MSNs firing together may more effectively mediate suppression between populations, in particular if these populations are also receiving sufficient background excitation from cortex and/or thalamus to keep them near the firing threshold (Ponzi and Wickens, 2010, 2013; Angulo-Garcia et al., 2016), possibly in a metastable depolarized 'up state' (Wilson, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Jaeger et al., 1994; Tepper et al., 2004).

claim: The magnitude of the constant external input can be used to control the rate of switching in the striatal model.
source: Figure 1c–d show that the expected sequence of activity (which is repeating due to the fact that we also depotentiate the weight between the last and first units) is indeed obtained in such a network, and that the magnitude of the constant external input can be used to control the rate of switching.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: The period of the activity sequence slows down tremendously as xin approaches the synaptic depression parameter β.
source: The period of the activity sequence slows down tremendously as xin approaches the synaptic depression parameter β.

claim: The external input from cortex and/or thalamus targets the particular subset of MSNs needed to express a particular behavior.
source: We can extend the model described so far to multiple—and even overlapping—behaviors by positing that the external input from cortex and/or thalamus targets the particular subset of MSNs needed to express a particular behavior.
evidence: The claim is a theoretical proposition based on the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model dissociates the computations of the selection and expression of motor sequence behaviors.
source: This model dissociates the computations of the selection and expression of motor sequence behaviors. The inputs to striatum select a sequence (possibly composed of several subsequences) by targeting a certain subpopulation of MSNs, and then the striatum converts this selection into a dynamical pattern of neural activity that expresses the behavior in time.
evidence: The claim is based on the theoretical model presented in the manuscript.

claim: A striatal network with initially random connectivity can learn to produce sparse sequential activity patterns when driven by time-dependent cortical input.
source: A striatal network with initially random connectivity can learn to produce sparse sequential activity patterns when driven by time-dependent cortical input.

claim: After the network has been trained, it is able to reproduce the same pattern of activity even after the time-dependent input is replaced by a constant excitatory input to all units.
source: After the network has been trained in this way, it is able to reproduce the same pattern of activity even after the time-dependent input is replaced by a constant excitatory input to all units.

claim: The model has the advantage of being able to dynamically adjust the speed of the activity sequence.
source: Compared with these earlier works, our model has the advantage of being able to dynamically adjust the speed of the activity sequence, as shown in Figure 4e (cf. however Refs. [Veliz-Cuba et al., 2015; Pehlevan et al., 2015; Tristan et al., 2014], where some temporal rescaling in activity patterns has been obtained using distinct mechanisms).

claim: The model does not require the assumption of heterosynaptic competition limiting the summed synaptic weights into and out of each unit.
source: In addition, our model does not require the assumption of heterosynaptic competition limiting the summed synaptic weights into and out of each unit, as in Ref. (Fiete et al., 2010).

claim: Time-varying input can lead to robust activity sequences, but this input is no longer necessary once the circuit has internalized the sequence.
source: Taken together, the above results show, within the context of a highly simplified network model, that time-varying input can lead to robust activity sequences, but that this input is no longer necessary once the circuit has internalized the sequence.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the results from the model presented in the manuscript.

evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the model structure.

claim: Sparse connectivity between neurons is sufficient to enable one population to effectively inhibit another.

evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Similar sparse sequential activity patterns have been observed in motor cortex in rodents performing a learned lever-press task.
source: In addition, while the highly structured input used to train the network may at first appear highly artificial, we point out that similar sparse sequential activity patterns have been observed in motor cortex, which is a main input to striatum, in rodents performing a learned lever-press task (Peters et al., 2014; Dhawale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Peters et al., 2014; Dhawale et al., 2015).

claim: Once the weights have been learned, constant input is sufficient to induce the desired firing pattern in the network, with the magnitude of this input controlling the rate at which the pattern progresses.

claim: The spiking network is able to learn a firing pattern from an external source, and later autonomously generate the same pattern over a wide range of speeds.

evidence: The claim is a summary of the results from the spiking model presented in the manuscript.

claim: A network of excitatory units with shared inhibition can be made to produce variable-speed sequential patterns.
source: Although, motivated by experimental results involving the basal ganglia, we have developed a model of recurrently connected inhibitory units, the same basic mechanisms for sequence learning can be applied to obtain sparse sequential firing patterns with flexible time encoding in a network of excitatory units with shared inhibition, a common motif used to obtain sparse coding of both static and dynamic neural activity patterns in models of cortical circuits. Such a network can be made to produce variable-speed sequential patterns just as in the circuit with direct lateral inhibition studied above.
evidence: The claim is based on the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dynamic range of temporal scaling factors that can be obtained in the model with shared inhibition is somewhat more limited than in the model with direct lateral inhibition.
source: However, the dynamic range of temporal scaling factors that can be obtained in this case is somewhat more limited than in the model with direct lateral inhibition, with an approximately four-fold speed increase obtained in Figure 6b, compared with over an order of magnitude obtained in Figure 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 6b and Figure 1.

claim: A purely inhibitory network, such as the one realized in striatum, may provide an advantage over an excitatory network with shared inhibition if involved in variable-speed tasks requiring a large dynamical range.
source: This suggests that a purely inhibitory network, such as the the one realized in striatum, may provide an advantage over an excitatory network with shared inhibition if involved in variable-speed tasks requiring a large dynamical range.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of the two models.

claim: The ability to generate variable-speed sequential activity patterns may be relevant for various frontal and motor cortical areas.
source: The ability to generate variable-speed sequential activity patterns may be relevant for various frontal and motor cortical areas, which can be described by the circuit architecture shown in Figure 6a, and which can exhibit sparse sequences similar to those in striatum during time-dependent decision making and motor-control tasks (Harvey et al., 2012; Peters et al., 2014; Dhawale et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Harvey et al., 2012; Peters et al., 2014; Dhawale et al., 2015) and the model presented.

claim: The model may provide an explanation for recent experiments showing that sparse sequences of neural activity in striatum dilate and contract in proportion to the delay interval in timekeeping tasks.
source: We have presented a model in which a network of recurrently connected inhibitory units internalize stereotyped sequential activity patterns based on temporally patterned input. Moreover, the same activity pattern can be reproduced after learning even after removing the temporally patterned input, and the speed of the activity pattern can be adjusted simply by varying the overall level of excitatory input, without requiring additional learning. As a model of striatum, we suggest that it may provide an explanation for recent experiments showing that (i) sparse sequences of neural activity in striatum dilate and contract in proportion to the delay interval in timekeeping tasks (Mello et al., 2015), and (ii) motor cortex is necessary to learn new behaviors but not to perform already-learned behaviors (which are presumably directed at least in part by subcortical brain circuits such as the striatum) (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model and comparison with experimental studies (Mello et al., 2015).

claim: The model may provide an explanation for experiments showing that motor cortex is necessary to learn new behaviors but not to perform already-learned behaviors.
source: We have presented a model in which a network of recurrently connected inhibitory units internalize stereotyped sequential activity patterns based on temporally patterned input. Moreover, the same activity pattern can be reproduced after learning even after removing the temporally patterned input, and the speed of the activity pattern can be adjusted simply by varying the overall level of excitatory input, without requiring additional learning. As a model of striatum, we suggest that it may provide an explanation for recent experiments showing that (i) sparse sequences of neural activity in striatum dilate and contract in proportion to the delay interval in timekeeping tasks (Mello et al., 2015), and (ii) motor cortex is necessary to learn new behaviors but not to perform already-learned behaviors (which are presumably directed at least in part by subcortical brain circuits such as the striatum) (Kawai et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the model and comparison with experimental studies (Kawai et al., 2015).

claim: The network can rapidly switch between cortically-driven and autonomously-driven modes even after learning of a particular pattern has taken place.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3, the network can rapidly switch between these modes even after learning of a particular pattern has taken place, perhaps somewhat similar to the switching between the 'practice' and 'performance' modes of male songbirds in the absence or presence of a female, respectively (Kao et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on the model presented and comparison with songbird behavior (Kao et al., 2005).

claim: Important differences exist in rodents, monkeys, and humans between goal-directed and habitual behaviors.
source: It is also well known that important differences exist in rodents, monkeys, and humans between goal-directed and habitual behaviors (for reviews, see Refs. [Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Graybiel, 2008; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Jahanshahi et al., 2015]), and exploring the relation between these behavioral modes and the cortically and non-cortically driven modes described above is an important direction for future study.
evidence: The claim is described as well known and supported by citations to review articles (Yin and Knowlton, 2006; Graybiel, 2008; Dolan and Dayan, 2013; Jahanshahi et al., 2015).

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity is important for reward-based learning of motor behaviors in rodents.
source: Assuming that the function of cortical input is to select from a set of possible learned behaviors as illustrated in Figure 2, we can ask what might be the potential role of corticostriatal plasticity, which many studies have shown is important for reward-based learning of motor behaviors in rodents, making these synapses a likely site for reinforcement learning (Reynolds et al., 2001; Barnes et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to experimental studies (Reynolds et al., 2001; Barnes et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2009).

claim: Corticostriatal synapses are a likely site for reinforcement learning.
source: Assuming that the function of cortical input is to select from a set of possible learned behaviors as illustrated in Figure 2, we can ask what might be the potential role of corticostriatal plasticity, which many studies have shown is important for reward-based learning of motor behaviors in rodents, making these synapses a likely site for reinforcement learning (Reynolds et al., 2001; Barnes et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cited experimental studies (Reynolds et al., 2001; Barnes et al., 2005; Yin et al., 2009).

claim: The basal ganglia circuit is important for controlling the 'vigor' associated with movements.
source: If a behavior leads to a greater-than-expected reward, then a (possibly dopamine-mediated) feedback signal can cause the recently active corticostriatal synapses to be strengthened, making that behavior more likely to be performed in that particular context in the future, lowering the threshold for activation and possibly speeding up the activity sequence underlying a desired behavior, making the basal ganglia circuit important for controlling the 'vigor' associated with movements (Yttri and Dudman, 2016; Dudman and Krakauer, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies (Yttri and Dudman, 2016; Dudman and Krakauer, 2016).

claim: Corticostriatal plasticity is likely involved with action selection and degree of vigor, whereas MSN-to-MSN plasticity may be more important for encoding kinematic details of a given behavior.
source: Although the model that we have developed focuses on plasticity within striatum rather than corticostriatal plasticity, it is worth emphasizing that it is consistent with both types of plasticity being present, with corticostriatal plasticity likely involved with action selection and degree of vigor, whereas MSN-to-MSN plasticity may be more important for encoding kinematic details of a given behavior.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the model and existing knowledge.

claim: Recurrent synapses in medium spiny neurons potentiate when presynaptic spiking is induced without postsynaptic spiking.
source: Central to the model is the anti-Hebbian plasticity rule that enables the inhibitory network to learn sequential patterns. Experimental results on medium spiny neurons in vitro have shown that recurrent synapses do in fact potentiate when presynaptic spiking is induced without postsynaptic spiking (Rueda-Orozco et al., 2009), as one would expect from the second term in (2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to an experimental study (Rueda-Orozco et al., 2009).

claim: Both Hebbian and anti-Hebbian forms of STDP at inhibitory synapses have been found in other brain areas.
source: Both Hebbian and anti-Hebbian forms of STDP at inhibitory synapses have been found in other brain areas, as reviewed in Ref. (Vogels et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article (Vogels et al., 2013).

claim: The overall level of external excitatory input to the network should affect the speed of the animal's time judgement and/or behavior.
source: Our model also predicts that the overall level of external excitatory input to the network should affect the speed of the animal's time judgement and/or behavior.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dopamine may be able to cause a change of the sequence speed by modifying the synaptic depression parameter.
source: Alternatively, dopamine may be able to cause a change of the sequence speed by modifying the synaptic depression parameter (β in our model), and there is evidence from in vitro experiments that this indeed occurs (Tecuapetla et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is a speculation supported by citation to an experimental study (Tecuapetla et al., 2007).

claim: Changes in tonic dopamine levels should be able to effect temporal rescaling by modulating the input gain and/or recurrent synaptic depression.
source: Thus changes in tonic dopamine levels should be able to effect temporal rescaling by modulating the input gain and/or recurrent synaptic depression, and indeed there has already been some evidence that such dopamine modulation occurs (Soares et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model and supported by citation to an experimental study (Soares et al., 2016).

claim: The theory predicts that the neural activity pattern in striatum should be the same in trained animals before and after cortical lesions.
source: Our theory also predicts that the neural activity pattern in striatum should be the same in trained animals before and after cortical lesions and that this neural activity should play a role in driving the animal's behavior.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neural activity in striatum should play a role in driving the animal's behavior after cortical lesions.
source: Our theory also predicts that the neural activity pattern in striatum should be the same in trained animals before and after cortical lesions and that this neural activity should play a role in driving the animal's behavior.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The theory suggests that time-dependent variability in cortical input is likely to decrease as an animal becomes more expert at performing a task, or as it switches between behavioral modes.
source: The theory suggests that time-dependent variability in cortical input is likely to decrease as an animal becomes more expert at performing a task, or as it switches between behavioral modes.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model presented in the manuscript.
